opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the issue is really about what level of description you're operating at. There's this idea, going back decades, that if we could just copy the brain closely enough, intelligence would fall out of it, and neural networks are sort of the modern descendant of that intuition. But the brain is an extraordinarily complex system, and we still don't know which of its properties actually matter for intelligence and which are incidental details of biology. Is it the individual neurons? The precise timing of spikes? The neuromodulators, the glial cells, the way the whole thing is embedded in a body that's interacting with a world? We just don't know.

And the neural networks we build today aren't really mimicking the brain in any deep sense. They take a very loose inspiration (units connected by weighted links) and then they diverge enormously. So when people say "these systems are brain-like, therefore they'll be intelligent like us," I think that's a big leap. Even the analogy to the visual cortex, which is the strongest case people make, breaks down once you look at things like feedback connections, attention, and how humans form abstractions from very few examples.

The other piece is that intelligence isn't just something happening inside a skull. A lot of what we call understanding comes from being embodied, from having goals, from living in a social and physical world and building up concepts through that experience. Things like intuitive physics, causality, and the ability to make analogies. Simply replicating some architecture, without that developmental and experiential grounding, may not give you the kind of flexible, robust understanding humans have.

So my view is that mimicking the brain is a useful source of ideas, but it isn't a recipe. We need a much better scientific understanding of what intelligence actually *is*, what the core concepts and mechanisms are, rather than assuming that if we copy enough of the hardware, the rest will just emerge.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding comes from being embodied and interacting with the physical world, and that without this experiential grounding systems may lack flexible understanding.

r002.rationale: The response says understanding comes partly from living in a social world and building concepts through that experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we don't actually know what "mimicking the brain" would mean, because we don't understand the brain well enough to know which features matter. Neural networks were inspired by the brain, but the inspiration is really quite loose. A unit in a deep network is a very simplified abstraction of a neuron. Real neurons have dendrites with their own computational properties, neuromodulators, glial cells, timing dynamics, all sorts of things that we've abstracted away. So when people say a system is "brain-like," they usually mean it has layers of simple units with adjustable connections, and that's a very thin notion of brain-likeness.

But I'd actually push on the deeper assumption, which is that intelligence is something that lives in the brain alone. One thing that's become clearer to me over the years is how much intelligence depends on the body and on being situated in a world. Our concepts, even very abstract ones, seem to be grounded in physical experience, in metaphors drawn from moving around, manipulating objects, interacting with other people. Children learn an enormous amount about causality, about what objects do, about what other people want, before they ever learn language. If you take the brain as the thing to copy and leave out development, embodiment, and social interaction, you may be leaving out the parts that actually make the brain's computations meaningful.

And there's a third issue, which is that even if you could build a perfect copy of the brain's hardware, that wouldn't by itself tell you anything. You would have intelligence without understanding it. It would be a bit like having a working airplane with no theory of aerodynamics. One of the things I care about in AI is that it should help us understand what intelligence is, what concepts are, how abstraction and analogy work. Pure mimicry, if it even succeeded, would skip over those questions. And in practice, the systems we have now aren't brains, so when they fail in strange ways, as they do, we have very little principled theory to help us see why.

So I'd say the problem isn't that the brain is a bad thing to look at. It's that "mimic the brain" quietly assumes we know what to mimic, assumes the brain is the whole story, and lets us off the hook from actually explaining what intelligence is.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence depends on the body and being situated in the world, grounding concepts in physical experience and interaction with objects.

r002.rationale: The response identifies interaction with other people and social interaction as part of what gives intelligence and concepts meaning.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the first question is, what do we mean by mimicking the brain? We don’t yet know which features of the brain are essential for intelligence and which details we can abstract away. An artificial neural network is inspired by brains, but that doesn’t mean it works the way a brain does, or that making it bigger will necessarily give it the same abilities.

And the brain isn’t operating in isolation. It’s part of a body that acts in the world, learns from the consequences of those actions, and interacts with other people. Those relationships may be essential to how intelligence develops.

So brain inspiration can be very useful. But it isn’t, by itself, an explanation of intelligence. We still need to understand what makes a system able to form concepts, generalize to new situations, and make sense of what it encounters.

r001.rationale: It says intelligence develops through a body acting in the world and learning from the consequences, and that these relationships may be essential.

r002.rationale: It says the system interacts with other people and that these relationships may be essential to how intelligence develops.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s an assumption there that we know what it means to mimic the brain. We have a lot of knowledge about neurons and different brain regions, but we don’t really understand how those mechanisms give rise to intelligence. So which features do you need to reproduce? Is it the behavior of individual neurons, the way they’re connected, the interaction between the brain and the body? We don’t know what level of description is the right one.

And the brain doesn’t operate in isolation. It’s part of a body that develops and acts in a physical and social world. If you take some simplified aspect of neural processing and implement it in a computer, that can be very useful, but it doesn’t follow that you’ve captured everything that matters for intelligence.

I see the brain as a source of ideas, but those ideas still need to be tested. Calling a system brain-inspired doesn’t, by itself, explain what it understands or how well it will generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence involves a brain embodied in a body that develops and acts in the physical world, and that neural processing alone may miss what matters.

r002.rationale: The response includes the social world as part of the context in which the body develops and acts, connecting that context to what matters for intelligence.
